newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK government extends helping hand to Tung.
newsitem.headline: HK government extends helping hand to Tung.

text.p: The colonial government extended a helping hand to Hong Kong's future leader on Tuesday by lending him two key officials to guide him through the difficult task of forming his own administration.
Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa is racing against the clock to establish a government ready to take up the reins when more than 150 years of British rule ends in 112 days.

Hong Kong becomes a part of China at midnight on June 30 and Tung, a businessman with very little political experience, will step into the shoes of Chris Patten, the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong.

Patten and the British have pledged to assist Hong Kong's next leader although they have steadfastly refused to cooperate at all with a provisional legislature to be installed on July 1 in place of an elected chamber.

The Hong Kong government said it had agreed to transfer temporarily the secretary for home affairs and the director of information services to Tung's office from Wednesday -- which is budget day in Hong Kong.
Home Affairs Secretary Michael Suen would assist Tung in the nitty gritty details of setting up an administration to be grafted onto what will remain from the colonial era.
Public affairs chief Irene Yau, who was planning to retire, has agreed to extend her term until the end of June, the government said in a statement.
"I am very pleased with the additional staffing support which is much needed as work builds up in the lead up to the handover," he said in a statement.
Tung's decision to retain a considerable portion of the colonial government framework has been regarded with approval in Hong Kong.

The Shanghai-born former shipping magnate opted for continuity last month when he announced the reappointment of Hong Kong's top tier civil servants, including the popular and influential chief secretary, Anson Chan.
But Tung's endorsement of China's plans to dissolve the elected legislature, undoing in a stroke recent democratic reforms instituted by the British, had stoked anger in some quarters.
